articles.title: FAA says airplane departures can resume following nationwide ground stop
articles.text:
FAA says airplane departures can resume following nationwide ground stop – WABE
FAA says airplane departures can resume following nationwide ground stop
Atlanta Airport
National News
FAA says airplane departures can resume following nationwide ground stop
National News
DorMiya Vance
Associated Press
| WABE
November 13th, 2026
Updated November 13, 2026,
9:55 PM EST
A Delta Air Lines flight information display shows delayed and cancelled flights at Atlanta's Hartsfield-Jackson International Airport on Friday, July 19, 2024. (Matthew Pearson/WABE)
The Federal Aviation Administration says airplane departures can resume after the agency lifted a nationwide ground stop caused by communications problems.
The FAA had grounded all flights nationwide Friday afternoon, causing hundreds of flights to be diverted. Officials cited “extraordinary circumstances” caused by communications problems at regional air traffic control centers.
The nationwide ground stop was the first since January 2023, when a key FAA computer system malfunctioned, and the second since the aftermath of the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks.
The nation’s top homeland security official attributed the problem to a telecommunications outage and said there was no indication the communications failure was related to a cyberattack. Trump administration officials blamed “overloaded,” “outdated” systems.
The consequences were profound, disrupting potentially thousands of planned flights through at least late Friday night and upending travel plans for passengers.
Friday’s restrictions were imposed “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety,” according to an FAA notice. The agency was investigating a communication issue affecting the 22 regional air traffic control centers that direct planes en route between airports nationwide, said Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy.
International flights were being handled on a case-by-case basis, according to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, with some seen taking off Friday evening. Meanwhile, some flights within Alaska and Hawaii were not impacted, Alaska Airlines said.
How did Hartsfield-Jackson travelers react to the halted flights?
The nationwide flight halts left thousands of Hartsfield-Jackson International Airport travelers, including Alicia Geimer and Aaliyah Black, stranded without access to their luggage or essentials.
“We were supposed to board our flight, like around 4:35, and then they pushed it back 20 minutes, and then they came on and told us that we were stuck because something happened with the communications,” Geimer said.
Delta soon alerted flyers that they could claim their bags, which would take up to five hours, with no guarantee customers would receive them back. However, that proved to be unsuccessful.
“We went to Delta customer service, and they told us the whole system is down,” Geimer said during the flight halts. “Now we’re stuck.”
They decided to stay with family friends until tommorow, hoping to receive flight tickets once everything is resolved. The duo remained optimistic, even though they had been told that flights to their destination had all sold out.
In a public statement, Delta Air Lines announced that it is safely resuming operations, noting that while flights have started departing, it will take time to reset operations, including positioning aircraft and crews.
“We thank our customers for their understanding and our people for managing through this disruption,” the statement reads.
“Customers should monitor their flight status on the Delta app or delta.com for the latest information. Delta will provide customers with as much notice as possible about changes to flight schedules.

articles.title: Supreme Court will consider Trump’s executive order suspending asylum access at the southern border
articles.text:
Supreme Court will consider Trump’s executive order suspending asylum access at the southern border – WABE
Supreme Court will consider Trump’s executive order suspending asylum access at the southern border
Immigrants
Immigration
Politics
Supreme Court
Supreme Court will consider Trump’s executive order suspending asylum access at the southern border
Supreme Court
Associated Press
AP
November 13th, 2026
Border Patrol agents ask asylum-seeking migrants to line up in a makeshift, mountainous campsite after the group crossed the border with Mexico, Feb. 2, 2024, near Jacumba Hot Springs, Calif. (AP Photo/Gregory Bull, File)
The Supreme Court agreed Friday to consider President Donald Trump’s ban on asylum at the southern border, a pillar of the Republican president’s far-reaching crackdown on immigration.
The Trump administration is asking the justices to overturn lower court decisions that found it was illegal to block asylum applications following an executive order that called the situation at the southern border an “invasion.” The suit is the latest in a series of immigration cases before the high court.
Federal law allows people to seek asylum if they fear persecution in their home countries, no matter how they arrived in the U.S.
At the same time, it also lets the executive branch decide whether people are granted asylum. The Trump administration argues it can categorically deny asylum to migrants covered by the order and should not have to accept applications destined to be rejected.
Federal attorneys say yearslong processing times had previously contributed to a major influx of migrants at the southern border as many were released into the country while awaiting a decision.
“Since the proclamation took effect, border encounters have fallen by 93 percent, dropping to the lowest levels since the 1960s,” Solicitor General D. John Sauer wrote, calling the asylum restrictions “critical” to the effort.
But attorneys from the American Civil Liberties Union and several immigration rights groups counter that border crossings were already falling before Trump took office.
They say his executive order is an unlawful attempt to unilaterally “eviscerate” legal protections aimed at protecting people fleeing danger in their home countries.
The executive branch does decide whether to grant asylum, which allows people to live and work legally in the U.S. But those decisions are supposed to be made on an individual basis and the law doesn’t allow the president to unilaterally stop people from even applying, immigration attorneys argue.
“The plaintiffs in this case fled persecution and torture, including political imprisonment and threats from the Taliban,” said Keren Zwick, executive director of the National Immigrant Justice Center. “Yet, the Trump administration refused to honor its obligation to consider them for asylum.”
The ban was one of a series of immigration restrictions Trump rolled out upon his return to office in 2025. It has remained in place during the litigation.
The justices are expected to hear the case in the spring and hand down a decision by the end of June.
It’s the third major immigration case the high court will hear this term. The justices will also decide whether people can be swiftly deported to countries other than their homelands and if immigrants can be detained indefinitely during deportation proceedings.
The justices decided another asylum case in favor of the administration earlier this year, clearing the way for the Trump administration to potentially revive a “metering” policy that has been used to turn back immigrants at the border in years past.

articles.title: Van Hollen to challenge Schumer for Senate Democratic leader
articles.text:
Van Hollen to challenge Schumer for Senate Democratic leader
Van Hollen to challenge Schumer for Senate Democratic leader; Ossoff, Warnock noncommittal
Election
Jon Ossoff
National News
Politics
Raphael Warnock
Van Hollen to challenge Schumer for Senate Democratic leader; Ossoff, Warnock noncommittal
National News
Associated Press
AP
November 13th, 2026
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., (left) and Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md. (right) (Mariam Zuhaib and Nathan Howard/AP)
WASHINGTON (AP) — Democratic Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland said Thursday that he will run for Senate Majority Leader in the next Congress, setting up a challenge to Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer after the party swept to power in the midterm elections.
Van Hollen said in a statement that “the American people called for change” and that is why he is running.
“It’s now on us to meet this moment, and to do that we need new leadership,” Van Hollen said. “This is not about any one person — it’s about answering the call of the American people. That is why I’m running for Senate Majority Leader.”
Schumer has said he has the necessary support to win the race, which will be the first contested election for Senate Democratic leader in decades. The closed-door, secret-ballot election will be held in early December.
The question of whether to reelect Schumer has already divided the caucus and many senators have declined to say publicly how they will vote, even before Van Hollen entered the race. They have privately deliberated about what message to take from the election and many are torn — Schumer recruited many of the party’s winning candidates and raised money for them, but progressive groups are pushing for his removal.
Georgia’s two U.S. senators haven’t said publicly who they’ll support.
Sen. Jon Ossoff’s office wouldn’t comment when asked on Friday about his preference for Senate majority leader. Sen. Raphael Warnock was asked about Schumer and Van Hollen on Tuesday.
“I think we’re at an inflection point in our country,” he told CNN. “Voters are demanding that we stand up and fight for them, and so any member of my caucus that feels like they should lead in this moment, I look forward to hearing their case.”
Making the pitch for his reelection, Schumer has been working with Democratic senators one-on-one to form an agenda for 2027. In private caucus meetings this week, Schumer opened discussion on a broad plan for their first 100 days in power that included healthcare and tariff legislation and efforts to stop the Iran war.
“I’m going to win it,” Schumer told The Associated Press in an interview last week.
In a statement after Van Hollen’s announcement, Schumer said he welcomes any discussion about the future of the caucus.
“I’m proud of what we’ve accomplished together — 55 seats and counting is an amazing result — and I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic Leader,” Schumer said. “I look forward to leading our new Democratic majority and delivering for the American people.”
Divisions over Schumer have simmered over the last two years
While Schumer is the favorite to win, Van Hollen’s run exposes a rift in the party that opened in the spring of 2025, when Schumer was put on the defensive after he sided with Republicans on a spending vote.
Even as Schumer has redeemed himself within his caucus since then — leading them through a government shutdown last year and orchestrating huge wins in the election — many in the Democratic base are agitating for generational change.
Van Hollen, 67, is not that much younger than Schumer, 75. But he has positioned himself as a new face in the party. He has also said he is considering a run for president.
While most Democratic senators have either said they are supporting Schumer or are undecided, Van Hollen has at least two backers: Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan, who won a competitive election in his state last week, and progressive standard-bearer Bernie Sanders.
El-Sayed posted on X Thursday night that their majority will need “bold leadership.”
“I called on Sen. @ChrisVanHollen to lead our caucus as a candidate back in April because he leads with courage and experience,” El-Sayed wrote. “We need both right now. Which is why I’m proud to stand with him in his bid to lead our Senate majority.”
Sen. Sanders, an independent who caucuses with the Democrats, held a press conference Tuesday announcing he would not support Schumer. He posted Thursday night that the American people “want a Democratic Party that will stand up to powerful special interests, take on the billionaire class and fight for working families. That is why I am supporting Senator Chris Van Hollen to lead Senate Democrats.”
Van Hollen has not yet laid out his own agenda, but he has criticized Schumer for his ties to Israel and other special interests.
While Schumer has a long history of support for Israel, he has strongly criticized Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his handling of the war in Gaza.
Schumer says he has broad support
Several senators have said they are backing Schumer, including incoming Ohio Sen. Sherrod Brown, who beat Republican Sen. Jon Husted last week. Beyond the election wins, those who support him say being the leader is a difficult job, experience is necessary and Schumer has proven himself with legislative successes when they held the Senate under President Joe Biden.
“Why would you fire the manager when you just won the World Series?” posted Maine Sen. Angus King, another independent who caucuses with Democrats and votes in the leadership election.
“Chuck Schumer is one of the principal architects of the most successful election in modern history, and I see no reason to change the leadership that helped make that success possible,” King wrote.
Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto, D-Nev., also posted her support Thursday evening.
Cortez Masto said Schumer was key in “securing a historic majority. I will be supporting him as our Democratic leader.”
WABE’s Rahul Bali contri

articles.title: Gwinnett soccer twins detained by ICE
articles.text:
Gwinnett soccer twins detained by ICE
Gwinnett soccer twins held by ICE just days after sending their team to nationals
Gwinnett County
Immigration
Immigration Detention
Law Enforcement
Local
Gwinnett soccer twins held by ICE just days after sending their team to nationals
Immigration Detention
Sophia Qureshi
285 South
November 13th, 2026
Twin brothers Carlos and Luis Orta-Santoro, recent Archer High School graduates and soccer players. (Photo courtesy of the Orta-Santoro family)
Nicolas “Nico” Azcarate Florez, a senior at Archer High School in Gwinnett County, came home from soccer practice last week and was about to start on his homework when he saw a notification pop up on his phone.
A friend in one of his group chats – made up of fellow teammates and their parents – wrote that “the twins got arrested in Alabama.”
Those twins are Luis and Carlos Orta-Santoro, two recent Archer High School graduates and former Archer Tiger soccer players. They’d come to Georgia from their college in Alabama to visit their parents in Bethlehem.
Traffic stop leads to immigration detention
On Nov. 4, the 19-year-old brothers were driving back to school, where they are both freshmen, when they were pulled over in Lincoln, Alabama, a city where a 287(g) agreement is in place (a cooperation agreement between local law enforcement and ICE).
According to a press statement, Luis and Carlos were stopped for rolling through a stop sign. They were initially issued a warning, their parents said in the statement, but the encounter escalated to an arrest and an immigration hold; the boys were subsequently taken to the Pickens County Detention Center in Alabama.
They’re currently at the Pine Prairie ICE Processing Center in southern Louisiana, according to the ICE Detainee Locator.
It was “shocking,” Nico told 285 South. He’s always been close to the twins – playing on the same soccer team for several years, and attending the same church. Luis and Carlos had stopped by their old high school just before they headed back to Alabama.
“They wanted to say hi to me and a couple more teammates,” Nico said. “They wanted to talk about how their season was going and how they were excited for nationals.”
Just a few days earlier, Luis had scored in a penalty shootout for the Wallace State Community College soccer team, a strike that helped launch them into the Division II national tournament, which begins this weekend.
Originally from Venezuela, Luis and Carlos’s parents have said the twins have pending asylum applications, no criminal records, and work permits that are valid until 2030. ICE has reportedly said that the boys’ temporary permission to stay had expired.
285 South has reached out to ICE for comment, but as of publication, had not received a response.
Archer High community rallies for the twins
The detention of the twins has shaken their parents, but also the Archer High School community.
Earlier this year, dozens of students had planned an ICE Out protest and push Gwinnett County Public Schools to adopt stricter policies to protect students from federal immigration enforcement.
“I remember when I originally planned the protest, and then when I was able to convince a lot of the other students to join it, it was because we were seeing what was going on nationally, and we were just really worried about that,” said Nehemiah Hamilton, who was class president at the time, and is now helping the Orta-Satoro family advocate for the twins’ release. “But it’s like it’s slowly getting closer and closer and closer to everybody.”
Community members have organized a 5K on Sunday, Nov. 15, at Alexander Park in Lawrenceville to raise awareness about their detention. Dozens of people have donated a total of more than $20,000 through a GoFundMe launched to help the family pay for legal fees.
Friends describe life in custody and the twins’ play on the pitch
Nico has spoken to Luis and Carlos a few times, he said, since they’ve been in ICE custody. “They’ve been saying that they’ve been moved five times, so it has been difficult for them,” he said.
In an audio recording broadcast by a Venezuelan news agency, one of the brothers describes being shackled during transfers. “They took us like animals,” he says in Spanish. “They tied us at the waist with the handcuffs and shackled our feet.”
The twins are great players, said Nico. Luis played left back for the Archer Tigers, and Carlos played on the wing. They were “players that you could just give the ball to, and you would know that they would do something good with it,” he said. On the pitch, “if we needed them, we would know that they would be there to help us out of a sticky situation.”
Off the pitch, their community is now trying to do the same for them.
“We’ve been through so much with them,” said Nico. “They are our dear family…. they’re like brothers to us.”
This story was provided by WABE media partner 285 South.
